assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance of the first rank: the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and beyond. They have redefined what can be measured, enabling relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the road to a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group drove the systematic-uncertainty and stability records and the many-body clock work. The two-name list is clean and fits the supplied credit well. Other contributors (for example Hall and Hansch for combs, already recognised in 2005) are not on this list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: multiple independent labs have confirmed the performance at 1e-18, clocks are compared across continents, and the field is in the formal redefinition roadmap. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit Ye and Katori for clocks only, or also for the strontium-specific work of other groups, is a scope question I cannot settle from the list.
Exact priority dates for the magic-wavelength proposal are recalled from memory, not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision sensor, with gravimeters, gradiometers, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. It fits my view that physics progresses with what we can measure and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of atom interferometers with light pulses, Pritchard's first atom interferometers and Kasevich's inertial sensors and large-momentum-transfer devices form a defensible three-person set. Holger Müller is a strong later contributor, but I judge the three founding names to be better balanced. Chu already received the 1997 prize for cooling and is outside this list.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the laboratory with independent confirmations across several groups, and commercial gravimeters exist. Space-based and gravitational-wave-type applications remain prospective, which does not weaken the core recognition.
uncertainties: Priorities between early interferometer demonstrations from several groups (Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu and others) make the attribution contentious.
The balance between Bordé's theory and the experimental firsts is a judgement call, and the list does not settle it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED is the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors: strong coupling of a qubit to a resonator, dispersive readout and the transmon-in-cavity platform. It is a measurement and control technique that opened a whole field, and its impact on quantum technology is clear.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the theory proposal, the first strong-coupling experiment and the sustained development of the platform. This is a coherent triplet. The superconducting-qubit prize in 2025 (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis) overlaps in field, and relative credit to that earlier recognition could be contested.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent labs and industrial groups. Timing is good, though recognition of closely related macroscopic quantum tunnelling work in 2025 may make the committee hesitant to reward the same platform soon.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may reduce appetite for another prize here.
Details of Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf priority relative to Girvin and Yale theory colleagues are from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the Mott transition to fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopes, give programmable and measurable many-body systems. They are a genuine instrument for studying quantum matter with single-site resolution, and have had broad influence across condensed matter and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the Hubbard simulation scheme, and Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger delivered the decisive experiments (Mott insulator, fermionic Hubbard, microscopes). I chose the experimental trio because I weight demonstration over proposals, but the choice is a real trade-off against the theory pair. The list also holds five names, which makes a three-person limit painful.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups. Applications to unsolved Hubbard-model questions remain partly open, so the scientific payoff is still developing.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the theoretical founders (Cirac, Zoller) or the experimentalists is unresolved.
Quantum simulation of the fermionic Hubbard model at the lowest temperatures remains an open challenge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single defect spins in diamond are a precision-sensing and quantum-network platform, used for nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry, biological sensing and loophole-free Bell tests and entanglement of remote nodes. The measurement relevance is high.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup made the first optical detection of single NV centres, Awschalom the broader solid-state spin control, and Hanson the entanglement and Bell-test work. Lukin and Walsworth have major claims as well, so any three-name selection omits significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature in sensing, with many independent groups and commercial products. The quantum-network side is still a work in progress.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across at least five major figures, and the three-person cap forces a contested choice.
Commercial and practical reach of NV sensors beyond laboratory demonstrations is still limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg-blockade tweezer arrays have become a leading platform for programmable quantum simulation and neutral-atom quantum computing, with hundreds of atoms, high-fidelity gates and demonstrations of error-corrected logical qubits. Impact is large and growing quickly.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Lukin contributed the blockade-gate proposals; Browaeys and Lukin led the early demonstrations of blockade and the atom-array simulators. The three-name set is plausible, but Bernien, Endres, Regal, Weiss and others made central contributions to tweezer arrays that are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Somewhat premature: the key results are only a few years old, and the larger scale experiments are by few groups. Independent confirmation exists but the interpretation of computing advantage is still evolving.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the older platforms above.
Credit for tweezer-array assembly itself is outside the credited names, creating a gap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed vacuum injected into interferometers beats the standard quantum limit and is now routine in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, a direct case of a quantum technique improving a measurement instrument and astrophysical reach. It is easy to explain and has proven operational impact.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the theory of squeezed-state interferometry, Schnabel the early GEO600 and broadband implementation, and Mavalvala frequency-dependent squeezing and quantum-noise work in LIGO. Kimble and Slusher made the first squeezed-light experiments, and are only partly covered (Kimble is on the list but I did not select him).
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent deployment in several detectors, with demonstrated sensitivity gains. The close ties to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize could weigh in either direction.
uncertainties: The founding experimental squeezing results (Slusher and others) predate this list and are not all credited.
Whether the committee sees this as distinct enough from the 2017 prize is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom-light interfaces, from cavity QED photon-atom gates to EIT-based memories and quantum repeater building blocks, underpin quantum network concepts. I know the quantum memory literature well and judge this field to be scientifically rich, but the realised networks remain at demonstration level.
assessment.attribution: Rempe's single-atom cavity and network work, Kimble's cavity QED and DLCZ-type protocols, and Lukin's EIT and photonic-interface proposals form a respectable trio. As a compound field, it overlaps with the Haroche-Wineland prize and with the several rare-earth and atomic-ensemble memory platforms, which are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Mixed: the individual demonstrations are solid and confirmed, but the practical quantum-network payoff is not established. Recognition could be early.
uncertainties: The scope of the discovery is a compound and diffuse, so the prize motivation would be hard to write.
Efficiency and storage times in the best memories remain short of what a network would need.
